---
title: "Probability measures"
---

The sample space $\Omega$ specifies token outcomes, and the sigma-algebra $\mathcal F$ specifies measurable groupings. We now need a numerical assignment that does not contradict those objects. We call this requirement the **coherence problem**.

Basically, a probability measure assigns a number between zero and one to every measurable event. More specifically, a [**probability measure**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited) is a function

$$
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal F\rightarrow[0,1]
$$

that satisfies the probability axioms below. The triple

$$
\langle\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P}\rangle
$$

is a **probability space**.

```{r}
#| label: load-probability-measure-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
wh$outcome_id <- paste(wh$split, wh$sentence_id, wh$token_id, sep = ":")

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L, !anyDuplicated(wh$outcome_id))

N_total <- nrow(wh)
category_mass <- as.data.frame(
  xtabs(~ lemma + dependency_relation, data = wh)
)
names(category_mass)[3] <- "tokens"
category_mass$probability <- category_mass$tokens / N_total
```

## The empirical measure

The declared probability experiment samples one token uniformly from the finite extract. For every measurable token event $E$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(E)
\equiv
\frac{|E|}{|\Omega|}.
$$

Thus every token singleton has mass $1/|\Omega|$, and a linguistic event receives the sum of the masses of its member tokens. For the *ne* event $N$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(N)
=
\frac{1}{|\Omega|}
\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathbf 1\{L(\omega)=\textit{ne}\}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: compute-empirical-measure
p_ne <- mean(wh$lemma == "ne")
p_object <- mean(wh$dependency_relation == "obj")
p_ne_object <- mean(
  wh$lemma == "ne" & wh$dependency_relation == "obj"
)

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(sum(category_mass$probability), 1)),
  all(category_mass$probability >= 0), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    p_ne,
    sum(category_mass$probability[category_mass$lemma == "ne"])
  ))
)

c(ne = p_ne, object = p_object, ne_and_object = p_ne_object)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-empirical-measure
#| fig-cap: "Empirical probability mass assigned to each observed lemma–relation category."
category_mass$category <- paste(
  category_mass$lemma,
  category_mass$dependency_relation,
  sep = " × "
)

ggplot(category_mass,
       aes(reorder(category, probability), probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65") +
  geom_point(color = "#2C7FB8", size = 2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## The three requirements

First, every event has nonnegative probability:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal F.
$$

Second, the full sample space has probability one:

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.
$$

Third, probabilities add across a countable collection of pairwise disjoint events:

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_iB_i\right)
=
\sum_i\mathbb{P}(B_i).
$$

The six lemma–relation atoms are nonnegative, disjoint, and exhaustive in this extract. Their empirical masses thus sum to one, as the code verifies.

## Consequences of the axioms

The impossible event has probability zero. Since $\Omega$ and $\varnothing$ are disjoint and $\Omega\cup\varnothing=\Omega$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)
=
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)+\mathbb{P}(\varnothing),
$$

so

$$
\mathbb{P}(\varnothing)=0.
$$

Likewise, $B$ and $B^c$ are disjoint and exhaustive:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1,
$$

and thus

$$
\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-complement
p_not_ne_direct <- mean(wh$lemma != "ne")
p_not_ne_complement <- 1 - p_ne

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(p_not_ne_direct, p_not_ne_complement)))
c(direct = p_not_ne_direct, complement = p_not_ne_complement)
```

## Counts are not probabilities

The six raw category counts are data-derived nonnegative values, but assigning them directly as event probabilities violates normalization because their sum is the number of tokens rather than one. Dividing every count by the common total produces the empirical mass shown above. This transformation changes the scale while preserving relative mass.

The measure is empirical and conditional on the represented extract. Uniform sampling of its rows does not imply that the original sentences were independently and uniformly sampled from Turkish, nor does it turn annotation decisions into error-free linguistic facts.

A probability measure is a coherent numerical assignment to measurable events. The [next page](probability-concepts.qmd) uses additivity to distinguish mutually exclusive from overlapping linguistic events.

## Check your understanding

1. Use the visible code to compute $\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(L=\textit{kim})$.
2. Compute its complement both by filtering rows and with the complement rule.
3. Verify that the three lemma events are pairwise disjoint and exhaustive.
4. Explain why the raw count of *ne* tokens is not itself a probability even though it determines the empirical probability after normalization.

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\widehat{\mathbb{P}}(L=\textit{kim})=17/167=0.101796$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The complement of the *kim* event contains 150 rows, so filtering and the complement rule both give $150/167=1-17/167=0.898204$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The three lemma events have pairwise empty intersections, and their counts sum to $3+17+147=167$, so they are disjoint and exhaustive. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The raw *ne* count is 147, which is not normalized to $[0,1]$; division by the common total gives the empirical probability $147/167=0.880240$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
